title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, piece by piece, to find out what makes it tick.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about money, death, identity, and the great London dust-heap that connects them all.
It is also, in my view, one of the funniest and most disturbing novels in the language — sometimes in the same paragraph.
Over this series, we'll be reading it closely, arguing about it passionately, and quoting it at length — because the prose deserves it.
Joining me today are three readers whose company I'm very glad to have.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is essentially an architect of prose — she reads every sentence for the structural choices hidden inside it.
When Eleanor gets excited about a sentence, you understand why the sentence exists.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as X-rays of class power — he's interested in who benefits, who suffers, and what the machinery of wealth actually does to people.
He earns every strong claim he makes — with evidence, from the text.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and re-reads it the way other people re-listen to favourite records.
She cares about what the reading experience actually feels like — what's funny, what breaks your heart, what makes you stop and read a line again.
To all three of you — welcome, and thank you for being here.
It's a genuine pleasure — this is a novel I've wanted to talk about in public for years.
Our Mutual Friend is where Dickens's craft becomes almost reckless in its ambition.
He's doing things with character and comedy simultaneously that should cancel each other out — and they don't.
Take the passage introducing Sloppy in his new black suit — it's pure comic architecture.
Dickens writes that he stood before the Council, and I want to read this exactly as written:
"a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
That quadruple string of present participles — shining, winking, gleaming, twinkling — is doing extraordinary work.
The buttons aren't just visible — they're animated, almost mocking, and so is the prose.
And what I find striking is that the comedy is inseparable from the cruelty of the situation.
Sloppy's body defeats the tailor's art because poverty has shaped that body in ways wealth simply cannot paper over.
Dickens tells us the tailor received personal directions to conceal the buttons — and the buttons won anyway.
That's not just a joke about tailoring — that's the novel's thesis about philanthropy.
You can dress poverty up, but the underlying structure of the body — of the life — resists.
What gets me is that phrase — "the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted."
That's describing a hatband.
Dickens uses the full philosophical apparatus of the human mind to describe a fluted hatband — and it's completely right.
It's the kind of sentence that makes you laugh and then feel slightly guilty, because Sloppy is so earnest in that suit.
He doesn't know how he looks.
Caroline, that tension — between our laughter and his innocence — is exactly where I think Dickens is at his most technically cunning.
He wants us in two emotional positions at once.
That same double register appears in his portrait of Bradley Headstone later in the novel — but with none of the comedy.
There's a passage where Bradley sits rigid through the night, and Dickens writes:

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes."
Again that accumulation — deepening, haggard, whiter and whiter — but now it isn't comic at all.
It's the same grammatical structure deployed for tragedy.
Bradley is what happens when someone from the labouring class internalises the system's demands entirely and has nothing left.
He's educated himself into respectability — and that very respectability becomes a cage, then a furnace.
The charmed flame turning him old — that's not metaphor for its own sake.
That's the novel showing you what social aspiration costs when the aspiration is denied.
He burns from within because the system provides no outlet for what he is.
Reading that passage aloud, the rhythm slows you down almost physically.
You can't rush it — the syntax won't let you.
And that slowness is Bradley's condition — trapped, immobile, burning.
It sits in such contrast with the Wegg passage, where the comedy is almost pantomimic.
Wegg turning an imaginary grindstone outside Boffin's keyhole — and Boffin stooping at it within — is pure silent comedy.
Dickens writes: "he then laughed silently, and stumped home."
Those two verbs — laughed and stumped — carry the whole character.
"Stumped home" — Dickens gives us Wegg's wooden leg in a single verb without mentioning it at all.
That is the economy of a writer at the height of his powers.
And the silent laugh — he doesn't even give Wegg a sound to gloat with — makes the menace more complete, not less.
Three quite different moments from the novel — Sloppy's buttons, Wegg's grindstone, Bradley's vigil — and already we're seeing a writer who refuses to stay in one register.
That range — comic, gothic, tragic — is one of the things that makes Our Mutual Friend so hard to categorise and so rewarding to argue about.

In our next segment, we'll be pressing harder on those questions of money and identity that lie at the heart of the novel — and asking what Dickens understood about the corrupting power of inheritance.
Stay with us.

segments.title: The Machinery of Money: Dust Heaps and Social Decay

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart to see exactly how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside the machinery of money — the dust heaps, the begging letters, the hidden wills, and the masks men wear when greed needs a respectable face.
With me are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher who obsesses over the architecture of sentences — the structural choices that make a passage sing or sting.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — every institution a mechanism, every fortune a set of victims.

And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who came to this novel as a teenager and has never entirely left it — someone who notices what's funny, what's unbearable, and what demands to be read aloud.
Daniel, I want to start with you, because the dust heaps in this novel are so much more than a plot device.
What does Dickens want us to understand about the origin of the Boffin fortune?
What Dickens understands — and what the novel forces us to feel — is that every great fortune has its waste at the base of it.

Old Harmon built his pile from dust and refuse — from the city's own discarded matter — and the will that governs everything downstream is shaped entirely by that founding act of hoarding and exclusion.
Wegg reads out that will with grotesque relish, and the language itself is telling.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
The Crown receives everything because the man made no human ties — as if the state itself is the natural heir to a fortune built on lovelessness.
That is not sentimentality on Dickens's part — it is a structural diagnosis.
What strikes me is how Dickens uses Wegg's voice to deliver that indictment.
Wegg is himself a grotesque — a man literally selling pieces of his own body, who now profits from the dead man's paperwork.
The form of the legal document — flat, impersonal, very short — set inside Wegg's crowing performance — is a superb piece of ventriloquism.
The coldness of law and the warmth of human malice delivered in a single breath.
And that coldness radiates outward across the whole novel, doesn't it.
Because the people who suffered most under that original fortune were children.
Boffin's account of the young John Harmon — seven years old, sent off alone — is one of the passages I find genuinely difficult to read.
Dickens makes you feel the physical smallness of the child before you feel anything else.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind."
That repetition — little scanty, little scanty — it's almost a lullaby, except it breaks your heart.
And Boffin's telling of it is itself a class document.
Here is a servant — loyal, decent, entirely without formal power — and all he and Mrs Boffin could do was offer warmth for a few minutes at a fire.
Dickens gives Mrs Boffin a line that concentrates all of that helplessness into a single cry.
"I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
She would give the world — but the world belongs to Old Harmon, and she has none of it to give.
The emotion is real; the powerlessness is structural.
There's a sentence later in that passage where Boffin describes the boy's last look — and Dickens writes himself into a corner beautifully.
He says the boy looked up "as if it was in pain — in agony."
That self-correction — from pain to agony — is a narrator reaching for the right word and finding it one word later.
It's a technique that mimics Boffin's own struggling speech — but it also mimes genuine grief trying to be precise about itself.
John Harmon carries that history into adulthood, and there's a passage where he articulates — to himself, alone — exactly what he returned to England feeling.
Daniel, that interior monologue in chapter thirty — it seems central to everything we're discussing.
It's one of the most searching moments in the novel — and the form is as remarkable as the content.
John Harmon interrogates himself like a witness and a cross-examiner at once.
And what he names, with this rolling, accumulating syntax, is a catalogue of mistrust — every kind of mistrust money can produce.
"I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife."
Three repetitions of shrinking and mistrustful — the syntax enacts what it describes: a man drawing back from every direction at once.
He doesn't trust the marriage his father arranged, he doesn't trust himself — he suspects he is already becoming his father.
The phrase "mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious" — that stops me every time.
It's not external pressure he fears most — it's contamination from within.
The dust heap casts a shadow forward through time and inward into character.
And then that extraordinary self-cross-examination at the end — "Is that so? That is exactly so."
He holds himself to account with the rigour he wishes his father's world had shown to anyone.
What's so deft is that Dickens gives this soliloquy to the character who is, for much of the novel, narratively absent.
John Harmon is hiding — literally dead, in the world's eyes — and his most articulate moment is this private audit of his own conscience.
The hidden man and the examined man are the same sentence.
Let's turn now to the way money attracts parasites — because the novel is absolutely ferocious on this subject.
Eleanor, the chapters dealing with Boffin's incoming correspondence — what is Dickens doing there?
He is running a satirical taxonomy — categorising greed by species, the way a naturalist would catalogue beetles.
And the formal variety is extraordinary — he moves from aggregate statistics to a verbatim ducal letter to individual case-studies.
That letter from the Duke of Linseed is a masterpiece of compressed mockery.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Five words of pure physical description — no verb — and Dickens has already made you feel the self-importance of the thing before you've read a word of it.
And then the postscript — "The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas" — described as thoughtful, of course.
The deeper point is institutional.
The charities themselves are described as mostly in difficulties, yet mostly lavish in print and paper — the apparatus of benevolence consuming the funds benevolence is meant to generate.
What Dickens is anatomising here is philanthropy as a class racket — a way for the nobility to extract money from the newly rich by flattering them with association.
The Duke needs Boffin's money; Boffin apparently needs the Duke's name.
The whole transaction is described as friendly — lithographed by the hundred.
And then the individual beggars — which I find hilarious and then immediately uncomfortable about finding hilarious.
There is this one image that punctures every sentimental self-portrait these letter-writers construct of themselves.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is so unexpected and so exact — the reduction of something living to something processed, something that has lost all its original form.
These people are not lying, exactly — they are minced.
And Dickens is scrupulous enough not to let us feel entirely comfortable with the laughter.
The beggars threatening suicide at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday — the precision of the time is grotesque comedy.
But the cold potato and the flickering lucifer-match are real details of destitution, not pure satire.
Dickens keeps the material conditions visible even while he's making you laugh at the rhetorical excess layered over them.
That tension — between laughter and horror — runs right to the centre of the novel's financial world.
And nowhere more so than in Fledgeby — a man who constructs an entire system of masks to profit from other people's debt.
Daniel, the revelation that Mr Riah is merely Fledgeby's front — what does that say about the novel's understanding of financial power?
It's the novel's sharpest demonstration that financial power operates most effectively when it's invisible.
Mrs Lammle's warning to Twemlow is delivered with the precision of someone who has learned exactly how the system works by being crushed by it.
She says, simply and devastating:
"Mr Riah is his mask. It has fallen into Mr Fledgeby's hands."
Two short sentences — repeated for force — and the whole architecture of Fledgeby's deception is there.
A Jewish moneylender as the public face; a chinless English gentleman as the concealed owner of the debt.
The mask is not incidental to the system — it is how the system functions.
And Twemlow's vulnerability here is so painfully specific.
He's a gentle, honest man — and Mrs Lammle identifies precisely that quality as his weakness.
She tells him not to let his "credulity, in judging another man's truthfulness by your own, from being imposed upon."
Decency, in this world, is a liability — which is perhaps the most savage thing the novel says.
What makes it bearable — and what makes it art rather than polemic — is that Mrs Lammle is herself implicated.
She married for money and found herself married to a fraud.
She's warning Twemlow not out of pure altruism but out of something harder to name — perhaps a late instinct for honesty now that there's nothing left to protect.
The moral lucidity of the ruined is a recurring note in this novel.
The moral lucidity of the ruined — that's a phrase worth sitting with.

We've moved today from a child shivering in the wind outside a dust heap, through the grotesque comedy of begging letters, to a moment of late grace from a woman who knows exactly how the machinery works.
Our Mutual Friend never lets money be simple — it is always also a question of what it does to human character across time.
Thank you to Eleanor, Daniel, and Caroline — and we'll be back in our next segment to follow the river where all of this eventually leads.

segments.title: Bella's Mercenary Heart: Character in Collision

utterances.text: Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we're diving deep into one of Dickens's most psychologically complex characters: Bella Wilfer.
Bella begins the novel as a self-declared mercenary — a young woman who wants money above all else.
But the forces pressing on her — disguise, surveillance, class, and the slow poison of old wealth — make her transformation one of the novel's great achievements.
To unpack all of this, I'm joined by three wonderful guests.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads Dickens for the architecture — the way a single sentence can carry a whole chapter's moral weight.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who treats novels as anatomies of class power — and he has a great deal to say about what the old Harmon money actually does to people.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel for years and cares passionately about which characters get a fair deal from their author.
Let's begin with John Harmon's confession — his account of why he staged his own disappearance to, as he puts it, prove Bella.
What strikes me first about John Harmon's long confession is how carefully Dickens has constructed its syntax — it spirals inward, circling back on itself, mimicking the very trap it describes.
He isn't giving a linear account; he's reliving an accumulation.
And the key word Dickens uses is exactly that — 'accumulative.'
He had lapsed into the condition in which he found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances.
That phrase — 'the accumulative power of its separate circumstances' — is doing so much work.
It absolves Harmon of pure calculation while refusing to let him off the hook entirely.
The structure of the sentence enacts the very process it names — each clause piling onto the last.
Eleanor is right that the syntax is doing extraordinary work — but I want to push on what the accumulation is actually made of.
Because Dickens names it very precisely: it is the father's wealth that corrupts everything it touches.
Dickens writes — and this is devastating — that the thought came from
the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence.
'Never yet for good' — that is an absolute indictment of inherited capital.
Harmon's psychological damage isn't individual — it is the systematic product of a system that turns human beings into instruments of property transfer.
And Bella, of course, is the most visible instrument in that system — the woman who was literally bequeathed alongside the money.
I want to stay with Bella for a moment — because I think the text is actually quite hard on her here, and it's worth asking whether that's fair.
Harmon admits he heard from her own lips that the marriage would have been thoroughly mercenary.
But he also knows, from the same passage, that she 'rejected his advances and resented them' when he appeared as Rokesmith.
So she's being judged for her mercenary words and simultaneously tested — watched — by a man she has never been allowed to know.
The plot Harmon devised with Radfoot is described as getting common sailors' dresses and throwing themselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood.
the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.
She is being surveilled before she has any idea the game has begun.
That should unsettle us, even as we're meant to find the scheme romantic.

Caroline has put her finger on something structurally fascinating: Dickens gives the 'proving' scheme to Harmon in a passage of free indirect thought — it isn't narrated as fact, it's narrated as Harmon's rationalisation.
And then Harmon actually cross-examines himself — 'I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right.'
That insistence on accuracy is the most revealing moment — because it flags exactly the reader's unease.
Why does he need to reassure himself?
Dickens is giving us, beneath the confession, the sound of a man constructing a self-justification in real time.
And that self-justification has a class dimension that I don't think we can ignore.
Harmon's dread is of perpetuating what he calls 'the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches — the fate that they should lead to nothing but evil.'
the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.
'Proving Bella' — as though she were a theorem, or a contract clause.
The language of property and legal proof bleeds directly into the language of romantic evaluation.
Dickens knows exactly what he's doing — this is the novel's great exposure of how capitalism colonises the intimate.
But I want to bring in something that I think the novel is quietly doing alongside all this moral anatomy — and that's showing us what money and drink actually produce, at the very bottom.
There's a passage from earlier — Lizzie Hexam describing a child in the household — that for me anchors everything about what Bella is escaping from, and what she could so easily become.
Lizzie says of this child:
This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.
'If she ever had one' — that small, almost parenthetical clause breaks my heart every time.
Lizzie doesn't labour it; she doesn't need to.
The doubt about whether this child ever had a cradle is the whole novel's case against what inherited poverty and drink do to human beings.
Caroline, that 'if she ever had one' is a masterclass in implication — Dickens withholds the sentiment and lets the syntax do the weeping.
And the father being described as 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — notice the rhythm: weak, wretched, trembling.
Three adjectives, each heavier than the last, before the final absolute: 'never sober.'
But then Lizzie adds — 'But a good workman too, at the work he does.'
That single concession is the mark of Dickens at his most humane — and most devastating.
And it connects directly back to Harmon's dilemma — because both situations are produced by the same logic: money that warps everything it touches.
I want to end with a moment that I find both hilarious and deadly serious — Boffin's tirade against the patronage economy of charity.
Boffin is now swimming in solicitations, and he explodes:

Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!
The accumulation of titles is the joke — and the indictment.
Dickens shows us that what passes for benevolence in this world is actually a system for purchasing social prestige with five shillings.
This is what Bella's mercenary instinct is embedded in — a culture where everything, including virtue, has a price and a title to go with it.
And what I love about Boffin's outburst is that it's delivered to Bella — she's in the room.
She's hearing a man she has come to genuinely love expose the absurdity of the very world she once aspired to join.
That, for me, is where her transformation lives — not in a speech she gives, but in these accumulated moments of education.
Eleanor, Daniel, Caroline — this has been a genuinely illuminating unpacking of some of the novel's most intricate territory.

We've moved from the Harmon money as a corrupting inheritance, through Bella as a surveilled subject, to the comedy and horror of Victorian philanthropy — and found they're all threads in the same knot.
After the break, we'll turn to the river — and what the Thames is doing to every character who comes near it.

segments.title: The Drowned Man's Secret: Plot, Disguise, and Narrative Games

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We're diving today into the novel's extraordinary narrative machinery — the disguises, the secrets, the way Dickens plays with what we know and when we know it.
With me are three readers who bring very different lenses to this book.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who reads for craft — the architecture of sentences, the structural choices that make a novel breathe.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of power — who benefits, who suffers, and why.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who brings a close ear to the verbal music and a fierce loyalty to the characters.
Let's begin with Boffin — and that extraordinary scene where he recounts his history with the Harmon family to Mortimer Lightwood.
What strikes me first about that scene is the voice — Boffin's voice — which is so alive on the page you almost forget you're reading a report of events.
He's telling Lightwood something genuinely dark: that John Harmon was mistreated, that there's real violence in this family history.
And yet the way he tells it — with that wonderful digression about Mrs Boffin's bonnet — it's almost comic.
Listen to how he puts it.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard."
That parenthesis — 'she wore, in general, a black straw' — is doing something extraordinary.
It humanises Mrs Boffin so completely, in one small detail, that when we reach the horror of what follows, we feel it as a real blow.
Caroline is absolutely right, and I'd push it a step further.
The parenthesis isn't just characterisation — it's Boffin's syntax performing his loyalty.
He can't narrate violence against Mrs Boffin without stopping to love her, in mid-sentence.
And then the sentence lands: 'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
Two words repeated. Full stop. The rhythm of shock.
Dickens knows that the shortest sentence in the paragraph will carry the most weight — and he earns it by making us wait through all that wonderful texture.
What I keep returning to is the political charge of that phrase: 'the poor boy gets no good of it.'
Boffin is stating something that the whole novel orbits — the inheritance system is designed to reward the dead, not the living.
Old Harmon uses money as a weapon of control across generations.
And when John Harmon finally seems about to receive what's his — as Boffin puts it — he is 'made away with, at the moment when he's lifting the cup and sarser to his lips.'
That image — the cup about to touch the lips — is not accidental. It's the structure of class deprivation made visceral.
The system promises; it withholds; it destroys. And then it moves on to the next heir.
That tension between inheritance and identity runs all the way through to John Harmon's disguise — his deliberate choice to remain dead, in a sense, and watch.
Eleanor, I want to bring you to Eugene Wrayburn — a very different kind of self-concealment, but equally fascinating from a craft perspective.
Eugene is one of the great examples in this novel of a character whose self-knowledge is perfectly precise and perfectly useless.
Lightwood tries to nudge him toward the future, toward consequence — and Eugene simply intercepts the thought.
'Look on to the end—' Lightwood begins, and Eugene catches the words immediately.
"That's exactly what I am incapable of doing."
Seven words. Absolute clarity about his own incapacity.
And the narrator tells us he says it 'with a perplexed and inquisitive face, as if he actually did not know what to make of himself.'
That 'as if' is doing crucial work — it allows the narrator to stay agnostic about whether Eugene's performance is genuine or strategic.
I find Eugene both infuriating and completely irresistible — which is, I think, the intended effect.
He won't plan, he won't commit, he drifts — and yet when the blow comes, there's something in him that refuses to give way entirely.
But contrast that with Bradley Headstone, who is incapable of not planning — who is consumed by consequence.
The passage about his psychological state after the attack is one of the most disturbing things in the novel.
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
The horror is that word 'efficiently.' He's not haunted by guilt — he's haunted by the thought of having made technical errors.
That passage enacts something profound about the social formation Bradley comes from.
Bradley is the respectable working-class man who has clawed his way into educational authority — every inch of his identity is built on self-discipline and performance.
So when passion explodes through all that self-control, his mind can only process it in the same register: how could I have done this better?
And Charley Hexam — who built his own respectability on Bradley's example — turns on him with extraordinary coldness.
Charley tells him: 'you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me.'
And the devastating irony is that Charley is himself the most perfectly selfish character in the book.
Two men who built themselves from scratch, and each accuses the other of the same crime.
And running beneath all of this — the disguises, the psychological torment, the accusations — there is that extraordinary train passage.
Dickens uses the train crossing the river as something close to a formal statement about time and fate.

"The train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
The train tears through everything — house-tops, streets, the earth itself — and then it simply crosses the river and vanishes.
And then the narrator steps back and gives us Father Time: going straight to his end, indifferent to what the water does beneath him.
That's the novel's secret plot, running under all the games of disguise: time is the only unstoppable force, and the river is its image.
That passage always makes me stop reading for a moment.
It's almost unbearably beautiful in context — because we know what that train journey is heading toward.
Dickens gives the river everything: it reflects light, it grows weeds and flowers, it turns and doubles — and none of it matters to that train.
Which is not quite nihilism. It's something stranger — a tenderness for the river's small life, alongside that brutal forward momentum.
The industrial technology moving through a landscape of demolished homes — houses torn down to make way for it — that is not a neutral image.
Progress in this novel always has victims. The train moves; someone's house comes down.
And yet Dickens doesn't let it be simply an indictment. The rocket metaphor is genuinely thrilling — that's part of the honesty.
He holds both things: the excitement of the new and the cost it extracts from the people in its path.
The river, the train, the money, the disguise — all of it converging on what the novel does with time and consequence.

In our next segment, we'll turn to the social world of the novel — the dinner tables, the drawing rooms, the Veneering set — and ask what Dickens is really saying about how respectability is manufactured and sold.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the novel's darker currents — the river, the dust, the dead.
But Dickens is also, page for page, one of the funniest writers in the language.
And the comedy in this novel is never innocent — it's doing serious moral work.
Caroline Woodcourt has been living with these passages, and I can think of no one better to open this up.
Caroline — where do you want to start?
I want to start with the Lammles, because the comedy there is almost unbearably sharp.
They are performing happiness for their guests — this perfect pantomime of marital warmth.
And Dickens knows exactly what he's doing when he sets up what follows.
He writes:
'How delightful those interchanges, and the looks accompanying them! Now, if the skeleton up-stairs had taken that opportunity, for instance, of calling out "Here I am, suffocating in the closet!"'
The joke lands because it's so precise — "suffocating" is the exact right word.
The skeleton isn't just hidden; it's being smothered by the performance itself.
What I love about that sentence is the mock-Gothic relish Dickens is playing with.
The skeleton in the closet was already a familiar Victorian idiom — he's weaponising the cliché.
But then he makes the skeleton speak — in the first person, in protest.
That shift from figure to voice is the move of a novelist who genuinely trusts his readers.
He doesn't explain the joke; he just does it and moves on.
And the skeleton is specifically financial — it's their fraud, their fabricated wealth.
So what's suffocating in that closet is the entire fiction that respectable society runs on.
The Lammles are only an extreme version of what the novel shows everywhere: the performance of solvency.
And comedy is Dickens's way of making that visible without having to argue it directly.
That idea about comedy as exposure connects beautifully to the Deputy Lock passage.
Here Dickens is doing something almost cruelly precise.
The Deputy takes Betty Higden's coins — pocketing them one by one — while delivering a speech about honest labour.
Let me read it, because the stage direction inside the dialogue is everything:

'I'm a man as earns his living by the sweat of his brow; here he drew his sleeve across his forehead, as if this particular portion of his humble gains were the result of sheer hard labour and virtuous industry; and I won't stand in your way. Go where you like.'
That parenthetical gesture — wiping his brow — is the whole novel in miniature.
The performance of virtue occurring simultaneously with the act of theft.
That parenthetical is extraordinary craft.
Dickens embeds the narrator's mockery inside the character's own speech — not after it, inside it.
The phrase "as if this particular portion of his humble gains" — that "as if" is doing all the work.
It exposes the gap between the claim and the reality without the narrator ever stepping forward to say so.
It's free indirect irony — the narrator ventriloquising the character's self-deception back at them.
And Betty Higden is there, receiving all of this.
She's a woman running from the workhouse — she is literally fleeing the institutions that claim to help the poor.
And this official — this Deputy Lock — extracts payment from her vulnerability while lecturing her on hard work.
The comedy is savage because its target is institutional hypocrisy of the most concrete kind.
He dismisses her with 'Go where you like' — the cruelest possible freedom, from a system that has nowhere good to send her.
I want to turn to the John Harmon identity passage, because it's doing something tonally quite different.
This is Harmon revealing — to the reader, not to any other character — the layers of his disguise.
The passage accumulates the identities like a set of Russian dolls.
Listen to how the syntax itself performs the multiplication:
'became as like that same lost wanted Mr Julius Handford, as never man was like another in this world.'
And then Dickens repeats the formula — nearly word for word — for Rokesmith.
The repetition isn't laziness — it's the joke, and the gothic horror at the same time.
The formula "as never man was like another in this world" — that's doing something wonderful logically.
It means: he resembles himself perfectly.
And by applying the same formula twice, Dickens makes identity itself collapse.
If Harmon is like Handford as no man was ever like another, and Rokesmith is like Handford in exactly the same way — then which one is real?
The comedy and the existential vertigo are absolutely inseparable.
It also raises something about the novel's treatment of legal identity.
Harmon is "lost" and "wanted" — both legally absent and legally hunted.
The law requires a fixed, legible self — a name, a face, a known address.
Harmon's multiple identities are funny, yes — but they're also a form of freedom from property law, from inheritance, from the whole system he's been born into.
And then there's Wegg.
If the Lammles are the novel's most elegant fraudsters, Wegg is its most magnificently petty villain.
And his come-uppance is pure, unapologetic physical comedy.
The moment Harmon grabs him, Dickens writes:
'he found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there.'
That list of verbs — gripped, shaken, shoved, pinned — each one a stage direction.
It's almost cartoonish — and entirely satisfying.
What I notice is the rhythm — Dickens uses the semicolons like punches.
Each clause lands separately, so the reader feels the accumulation of physical force.
"Shaken until his teeth chattered" — that's onomatopoeic almost; you can hear Wegg's humiliation.
And "sarcastic retort" — the phrase he's mid-sentence on when he gets grabbed — that's the joke.
His pomposity is literally stopped in its tracks.
There's something important about what triggers the violence, though.
Wegg is using language as a weapon — sarcasm, insinuation, the rhetoric of the petty blackmailer.
And Harmon — who has wealth, legal standing, the full weight of property behind him now — responds with brute force.
It's comic, but it also shows how power ultimately doesn't argue — it grips and pins.
Even when we're laughing, Dickens is watching where the force actually lies.
Daniel, that's a beautiful and slightly uncomfortable note to pause on.
Comedy as exposure, comedy as rhythm, comedy as the place where power shows its teeth.
What this conversation makes clear is that in Our Mutual Friend, there is no such thing as a purely innocent laugh.
In our next segment, we'll be looking at how Dickens uses the Thames — and everything the river carries — as a moral landscape.

segments.title: Society's Reflection: Class, Character, and the Novel's Architecture

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart to see how it works — and why it still matters.
Our Mutual Friend is a vast, intricate machine — part social satire, part gothic thriller, part love story — and today we're asking how Dickens builds its moral architecture.
How does he distribute virtue and degradation across his characters, and what does that distribution tell us about the society he's anatomising?
Joining me today are three extraordinary readers of this novel.
Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative-writing teacher whose eye for structural craft is, frankly, unsettling in its precision.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and he earns every word of his anger with evidence.
And Ms Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived inside this novel since her teens and knows exactly which sentences deserve to be read aloud slowly.

Daniel, I want to start with you, because you've been thinking about what Dickens says about good and evil — not through plot, but through a direct authorial statement that I find genuinely arresting.
Thank you — yes, because the passage I've been sitting with is one of those moments where Dickens steps directly in front of the curtain and tells you what he believes.
He's talking about the Boffins — Noddy and Henrietta — two people the novel codes as ignorant, unpolished, working people who have somehow remained morally straight.
And what he says about the force that exploited them is remarkable — that it had been, quote, 'never so warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it.'
The system that wrings maximum work for minimum pay is compelled, despite itself, to acknowledge virtue in the people it crushes.
Then Dickens delivers what I'd call his eternal law — and I want to read it, because it has to be heard whole.
'For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.'
Six words at the end: 'but Good, never.' That's the whole argument compressed to almost nothing.
And what interests me politically is that Dickens locates this indestructible good not in a gentleman or a philanthropist — but in two working people whom the novel's elite would barely register.
What Daniel is pointing to architecturally is extraordinary — that Dickens inserts this axiomatic statement mid-narrative, almost like a theorem being proved by the characters around it.
The rhetorical shape of that sentence is itself doing moral work — the long accumulated clause about evil, then the absolute truncation: 'but Good, never.'
Dickens knows that brevity, in that position, lands harder than any elaboration could.
And it sets up a structural counterweight that runs through the whole novel — because when we see degradation and suffering, this law is quietly operating in the background.
I keep returning to the phrase 'in its own despite' — that the hard, exploitative nature respected the Boffins' goodness despite itself, in constant conflict.
There's something almost tragic in that — the system knows what it's destroying, and does it anyway.
But the Boffins survive it, and that survival matters enormously to the emotional life of this novel.
Daniel, you've also been looking at a very different kind of scene — a moment of physical degradation that the novel presents in almost gothic terms.
Can you talk us through what happens when Mr Dolls and Eugene Wrayburn share a scene at Jenny Wren's?
This is one of the cruelest juxtapositions in the novel — and it's cruel in a way that I think Dickens is entirely aware of.
You have Jenny Wren's father — a man destroyed by poverty and drink, his body barely responding to his own will — and you have Eugene Wrayburn, idle, privileged, lighting his cigar.
Dickens renders the father with a kind of forensic pity — listen to this:
'The miserable man, feebly rubbing the back of his faltering hands downward from the wrists, shuffled on to his post of disgrace.'
'Post of disgrace' — that is the novel naming the social sentence passed on this man as if it were judicial, official, permanent.
And then Eugene departs with 'a lazy compliment or so' — not cruelty exactly, but a complete indifference that is its own form of violence.
The two men occupy the same room, but they might as well be on different planets — and the novel knows it, and wants us to feel the gulf.
That phrase 'if any action of any limb or joint he had, would have answered truly to his will' — that subordinate clause does something devastating.
It locates his degradation not in his will but in his body's betrayal of it — there's still a self in there, trying to make a gesture toward Eugene.
Dickens denies him the dignity of completing even a small, ambiguous action — and that denial is the point.
And Eugene's response — 'instinctively falling away from the disagreeable contact' — is so precisely observed it makes you wince.
It's not contempt, it's worse — it's reflex. The man doesn't even rise to the level of conscious disdain.
Eugene is charming and funny elsewhere in the novel, which makes this moment all the more uncomfortable.

Let's hold that discomfort — because Daniel, you've been thinking about a very different emotional register: a meal scene involving Bella Wilfer, John Rokesmith, and her father that is almost fairy-tale in its warmth.
How does that happiness function in a novel so preoccupied with class and suffering?
It functions as counterpoint — and as a kind of utopian glimpse, which Dickens earns by being so precise about its material conditions.
The meal takes place in an office — the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring from the corner.
Commerce and capital are literally watching this domestic happiness — described as 'the eyes of some dull dragon.'
And yet Dickens insists the happiness is real — let me read the passage, because the fairy-tale comparison is doing serious work here:

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
The fairy tale is invoked — but with the threat removed. No growling. No territorial rage over property.
That is precisely what Dickens imagines a good society might feel like — abundance without the primal snarl of possession.
What moves me is that little parenthetical — 'as Bella gaily said.' It's Bella's simile, not the narrator's.
She's the one who finds the fairy tale in the moment — and that's her whole character arc, isn't it? Learning to find delight in small things rather than chasing the golden dustheap.
And 'even R. Wilfer' — that 'even' is so tender. Her father has known so little pleasure that his inclusion here carries enormous weight.
The 'uncongenial oddity of its surroundings' making the meal 'the more delightful' — that's a really sophisticated structural choice.
Dickens is saying joy is not diminished by ugly surroundings — it is intensified by them. The contrast is generative.
And that principle ripples through the whole architecture of the novel — virtue and warmth and love appearing precisely in the places the world would least expect them.
And then we turn to one of the novel's most uncomfortable confrontations — Charley Hexam facing Bradley Headstone in the aftermath of violence.
Daniel, what does this scene reveal about guilt, complicity, and the way the novel distributes moral responsibility?
Charley Hexam is a character the novel treats with great psychological acuity — he's ambitious, calculating, and he has climbed away from his class roots with both hands.
And in this confrontation with Headstone, what he's really articulating is the cost of his own complicity — every alliance he made in the service of his ambition is now a liability.
Listen to how he frames it — there is a legal precision to his language that is almost chilling:
'You know that I took you with me to his chambers in the Temple when I told him my opinion of him, and made myself responsible for my opinion of you.'
He's not grieving Eugene's near-murder — he's enumerating how it has damaged him. That is a devastatingly clear-eyed portrait of a particular kind of social climber.
And then: 'Is that your gratitude to me, Mr Headstone?' — the moral vocabulary of gratitude deployed entirely in the service of self-interest.
The rhetoric of that speech — 'I don't say what,' 'I don't say how much,' 'I go no closer' — is extraordinary.
Charley is simultaneously accusing Headstone and protecting himself — each hedge is a tiny act of self-preservation dressed as scruple.
It's also a brilliant piece of Dickensian free indirect discourse — we're very close to Charley's calculating mind, and it's uncomfortable precisely because we understand him.
What always strikes me is that Charley has abandoned his sister Lizzie entirely by this point — and yet he couches everything in the language of duty and loyalty.
'Favouring your desire to marry my sister' — as if he were doing her a favour, when in fact he was using her as a bargaining chip in his own negotiations with Headstone.
Dickens gives Charley a very particular kind of corruption — not violence, not greed in the obvious sense, but an utter subordination of feeling to calculation.
And in a novel so interested in what money does to the soul, that is a quietly devastating portrait.

We've moved today from the eternal law that good outlasts the doer, through the gothic gulf between Eugene and a broken man, through fairy-tale joy amid commercial surroundings, and into the cold arithmetic of a young man's moral ledger.
What emerges is a novel that refuses to let any single register — sentiment, satire, gothic darkness — have the last word.
Thank you to Eleanor, Daniel, and Caroline — and we'll be back shortly to go deeper into the novel's strangest and most compelling corners.

segments.title: Closing: Mutual Redemption and Narrative Transformation

utterances.text: We've arrived at the final movement of today's conversation, and it feels right to end here — with the question of what this novel ultimately asks of us.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about transformation — who gets redeemed, who gets exposed, and who quietly slips through the cracks of the narrative's mercy.
Eleanor has been thinking about the architecture of Dickens's moral vision — how he arranges virtue, satire, and something close to the visionary all in the same novel.
What strikes me about the closing energies of this novel is that Dickens refuses to let virtue and fashionability coexist.
The Boffins are a case study in that refusal — and the passage that captures it is almost unbearably tender in its simplicity.
Mr Boffin turns to his wife and says, simply:
"Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!"
And then Dickens delivers the verdict with that perfectly calibrated irony:
"It was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, but, having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair."
That capital U on 'Unfashionable' — Dickens capitalises it as if it were a title of honour — is one of the most quietly devastating strokes in the whole novel.
The Boffins lose the social game precisely because they are good — and Dickens plants his flag right there.
Eleanor is right that Dickens plants his flag — but I want to push on where that flag is actually planted.
The Boffins are redeemed precisely because they refuse the logic of fashionable society — which is also the logic of extraction and display.
Contrast that with Wegg — who embodies the same logic taken to its grotesque conclusion.
Wegg's scheme against Boffin is laid out with almost bureaucratic precision — and it gives us the most naked articulation of what money means in this world.
He proposes that their price on the incriminating document is expressible in one word — and then delivers it:
"He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
And if Boffin steps out of line, Wegg promises something more sinister still:
"He should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions."
'Moral bondage and slavery' — Dickens gives Wegg the language of total domination, and it is not accidental.
This is what the pursuit of money produces: the ambition to own another person entirely.
I keep returning to a very different kind of vision in this novel — and it comes from the character who has least power and most pain.
Jenny Wren's passage about the celestial children is, for me, the emotional heart of any discussion of redemption in this book.
She describes how, when she was a small child — and she says it, as Dickens notes, 'in a tone as though it were ages ago' — she would see children unlike any others.
"They were not like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were never in pain."
And they called out to her — a refrain she never forgot:
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
That repetition — 'Who is this in pain' — it doesn't comfort by denying the suffering.
It names it, openly, and then offers not a cure but companionship.
For a child who has never been allowed to play, to be told 'Come and play with us' — that is the most radical form of grace this novel imagines.
Caroline has put her finger on something I find endlessly fascinating about Dickens's craft here — the way the vision is both utterly concrete and unmistakably spiritual.
Those children appear in 'long bright slanting rows' — it's a visual fact, almost architectural in its precision.
And then something extraordinary: Jenny says she's tried to imitate the shining on their borders and heads in her work — and she cannot.
The artist's hands cannot reproduce the vision.
I think that's Dickens's most honest moment about what fiction can and cannot do — it can point toward transcendence, but not contain it.
And notice who carries this vision — the child labourer, the doll's dressmaker, the one the novel refuses to sentimentalise into mere pathos.
Jenny Wren is 'chilled, anxious, ragged' — Dickens lists those adjectives as a social indictment, not a character description.
The visionary capacity belongs to her precisely because she has been denied everything that the fashionable world — the Wegg world — values.
And the contrast with Wegg's 'Halves!' could not be starker — his word for the world is a fraction; hers is 'Have patience, and we will come again.'
And she holds onto that promise — 'Have patience, and we will come again' — through everything the novel throws at her.
There's a kind of moral endurance in Jenny that doesn't come from anywhere the novel's plot rewards — no inheritance, no marriage plot resolves her suffering.
She simply persists, tending her imagined birds and flowers — 'I dare say my birds sing better than other birds,' she says, and you believe her completely.
That is a form of transformation too — not narrative rescue, but interior sovereignty.
Interior sovereignty — I think that phrase might be the best we've found today for what this novel is ultimately about.
The Boffins keep their goodness and lose the fashionable world.
Wegg reaches for everything and ends up enslaved to his own scheme.
And Jenny Wren — broken, working, waiting — holds a vision that the novel's wealthiest characters cannot purchase.
My thanks to Eleanor Hartley, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — for a conversation that has done justice, I think, to one of Dickens's most ambitious and searching novels.
Our Mutual Friend repays every reading — and I hope today has given you reason to return to it.

The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.

‘Exactly so, sir!’ returned Wegg, blandly and buoyantly. ‘I see I take you
      with me! Hear, hear, hear! Resolved, as your discriminating good sense
      perceives, that if you was to have a sap—pur— ize , it should be
      a complete one! Well, sir. And so, as you have honoured me by
      anticipating, I examined the document. Regularly executed, regularly

      Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, "I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.

Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
c40:p72.summary: Wegg proposes an elaborate scheme: let Boffin excavate the Mounds at his own expense while they observe, then when the work is done, threaten him with the earlier will and extort half his property. If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.
c40:p72.best_quote: That, he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' ... he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.

c19:p76.text:
‘I dare say my birds sing better than other birds, and my flowers smell
      better than other flowers. For when I was a little child,’ in a tone as
      though it were ages ago, ‘the children that I used to see early in the
      morning were very different from any others that I ever saw. They were not
      like me; they were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were
      never in pain. They were not like the children of the neighbours; they
      never made me tremble all over, by setting up shrill noises, and they
      never mocked me. Such numbers of them too! All in white dresses, and with
      something shining on the borders, and on their heads, that I have never
      been able to imitate with my work, though I know it so well. They used to
      come down in long bright slanting rows, and say all together, “Who is this
      in pain! Who is this in pain!” When I told them who it was, they answered,
      “Come and play with us!” When I said “I never play! I can’t play!” they
      swept about me and took me up, and made me light. Then it was all
      delicious ease and rest till they laid me down, and said, all together,
      “Have patience, and we will come again.” Whenever they came back, I used
      to know they were coming before I saw the long bright rows, by hearing
      them ask, all together a long way off, “Who is this in pain! Who is this
      in pain!” And I used to cry out, “O my blessed children, it’s poor me.
      Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!”’
c19:p76.summary: Jenny recounts a memory or vision from her childhood of celestial children in white who appeared to her, asking 'Who is this in pain?' and offering her comfort and rest. They promised to return, and their refrain became her solace.
c19:p76.best_quote: 'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'
